title: The Tenth Guru's book
hook: compiled after his death, traditionally by Bhai Mani Singh; its make-up is discussed respectfully among Sikhs

segments.voice: Yesterday the Gurus' teachings closed, from the second Guru through the fifth, and the ninth. Your line was one teaching, many voices.

Some books are finished by their authors. Others are finished by the people who loved them. A teacher dies, and a student goes from house to house, collecting copies of what was written, sorting them, setting them in order. The book that comes out of it is treasured. Because the teacher didn't set the order himself, readers can ask, gently, which page came from which hand. A new block of the path starts today, the writings of Guru Gobind Singh, and it starts with a book like that.
screen: `FINISHED BY THOSE WHO LOVED HIM.` → `COPIES GATHERED, SET IN ORDER.` → `WHICH PAGE, WHICH HAND?`

segments.voice: Its name is Dasam Granth: the book of the Tenth. You first heard that name on day eighty-three, at a court of poets in Anandpur. It holds writings associated with Guru Gobind Singh. Tradition says it was compiled after his death, and it names Bhai Mani Singh, a learned Sikh of the Guru's circle, as the one who gathered it. So it was not set in order by the Guru himself the way the Adi Granth was set in order by Guru Arjan. That difference matters, and Sikhs keep it in view. Inside, some of it Sikhs pray every day: Jaap Sahib, and verses from Akal Ustat, are among the morning prayers of the Sikh daily round, and tradition places some of its prayers at the Khalsa initiation. There is Bachitar Natak, a poem that tells parts of his own story. There is the Zafarnama, a letter in Persian. And there are long retellings of old Indian tales that read very differently from the hymns. The Guru Granth Sahib is the Guru for Sikhs; the Dasam Granth is not. Sikhs discuss which parts of the Dasam Granth come from the Guru's own pen. Some hold that all of it does. Some hold that the prayers clearly do and other parts may come from poets in his court. At its best, that discussion keeps a careful tone, because it's about a beloved teacher's words. Nobody on this path will be told which side to take. For the next weeks, this path reads the parts Sikhs pray and quote, and says plainly when a question is open.
screen: `THE BOOK OF THE TENTH.` · `GATHERED AFTER HIS DEATH.` · `PRAYERS, A LIFE, A LETTER.` · `NOT THE GURU; ITS MAKE-UP DISCUSSED.` · then, large: `DISCUSSED WITH RESPECT.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one question where honest people land in different places: a family question, a work question, a question of faith. Find one sentence about the people who see it the other way that they would recognize as fair. If you pray, rest in Waheguru for a few breaths.
Dasam Granth. The book of the Tenth: writings of Guru Gobind Singh gathered after his death, with daily prayers inside, and a make-up Sikhs discuss with care. Today's word.
Your line: discussed with respect. The writings of the Tenth Guru begin here, with the book itself. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Sikhs recite Jaap Sahib and verses from Akal Ustat, both found in the Dasam Granth, among their daily prayers; the Guru Granth Sahib alone is installed and honored as the Guru.

chat.says: Is the Dasam Granth the Sikh scripture that's honored as the Guru?
options: No. The Guru Granth Sahib is the Guru; the Dasam Granth holds the tenth Guru's writings.
Yes. It replaced the Guru Granth Sahib as the Guru after the tenth Guru died.
No. It's a modern history of the Gurus, written by scholars last century.
chat.meaning: The Guru Granth Sahib is the Guru for Sikhs; the Dasam Granth is not. It gathers writings associated with Guru Gobind Singh, compiled after his death.
